span.label: Operant conditioning as a process and as an experimental paradigm - how behaviour is selected by its consequences.
span.quote: Operant conditioning (also known as instrumental conditioning ) is a process by which humans and animals learn to behave in such a way as to obtain rewards and avoid punishments.

span.label: What is the relation between behaviour and its consequences, and how far does the analogy with natural selection actually carry?
span.quote: The scientific study of operant conditioning is thus an inquiry into perhaps the most fundamental form of decision-making.

span.label: Sets out operant conditioning as ontogenetic selection - behaviour varied then selected by reinforcement - and flags that the variation half of the analogy has gone unstudied.
span.quote: The view of operant behavior as a repertoire of emitted acts from which one is selected by reinforcement, immediately forged a link with the dominant idea in biology: Charles Darwin’s natural selection, according to which adaptation arises via selection from a population that contains many heritable variants, some more effective – more likely to reproduce – than others.

span.label: critique
span.quote: If our aim is to arrive at knowledge that will help us educate our children, then the overwhelming emphasis in the history of this field on selection (reinforcement), which was once appropriate, may now be failing to address some of the most important unsolved problems.

span.label: operant conditioning
span.quote: Operant conditioning (also known as instrumental conditioning ) is a process by which humans and animals learn to behave in such a way as to obtain rewards and avoid punishments.

span.label: review
span.quote: Most generally, current theories of operant learning can be divided into three main types -- those that attempt to accurately describe behavior (descriptive theories), those that are concerned with how the operant learning is realized in the brain (biologically inspired theories), and those that ask what is the optimal way to solve problems like that of assigning credit to actions, and whether such optimal solutions are indeed similar to what is seen in animal behavior (normative theories).

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Reinforcement is the selective agent, acting via temporal contiguity (the sooner the reinforcer follows the response, the greater its effect), frequency (the more often these pairings occur the better) and contingency (how well does the target response predict the reinforcer).

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: The general principle that emerges from these experiments is that the predictive properties of the situation determine the repertoire, the set of activities from which consequential, operant, reinforcement can select.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: A stimulus (like the CS) that predicts food generates via built-in mechanisms, a repertoire that is biased towards food-getting behaviors

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: But at the same time, the subject's repertoire becomes more limited, so that for many tasks the effective response may cease to occur if the situation is too predictive

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Because the probability a given response will be reinforced on a VI schedule declines the more responses are made – and increases with time away from the schedule – almost any reward-following process yields matching on concurrent VI VI schedules.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: It was nevertheless valuable because it introduced an important distinction between reflexive behavior, which Skinner termed elicited by a stimulus, and operant behavior, which he called emitted because when it first occurs (i.e., before it can be reinforced) it is not (he believed) tied to any stimulus.

span.label: The theoretical account is incomplete by the article's own statement - the empirical space is mapped, the mechanism is not.
span.quote: Exactly how all this works is still not understood in full theoretical detail, but the empirical space – the effects on response strength (rate, probability, vigor) of reinforcement delay, rate and contingency – is well mapped.

span.label: A century of research has studied selection and not variation: where the first successful response comes from is unexamined.
span.quote: Omitted is any discussion of where the successful response comes from in the first place.

span.label: The framework that organised the field is described as not really a theory.
span.quote: Skinner’s ‘theory’ was more an organizing framework than a true theory.

span.label: The credit-assignment problem is taken over from AI and made the central question that an operant conditioning process must answer

span.label: Darwin's natural selection is imported as the model for operant conditioning, with reinforcement as the selective agent acting on a variable repertoire of emitted acts
span.quote: immediately forged a link with the dominant idea in biology: Charles Darwin’s natural selection, according to which adaptation arises via selection from a population that contains many heritable variants

span.label: The reinforcement-learning framework is adopted as the normative account within which both Pavlovian and operant behaviour are interpreted
span.quote: The computational field of reinforcement learning has provided a normative framework within which both Pavlovian and operant conditioned behavior can be understood.

span.label: Darwinian selection from a varied population, imported to explain how one behaviour is picked out of an emitted repertoire by reinforcement
span.quote: The view of operant behavior as a repertoire of emitted acts from which one is selected by reinforcement, immediately forged a link with the dominant idea in biology: Charles Darwin’s natural selection, according to which adaptation arises via selection from a population that contains many heritable variants, some more effective – more likely to reproduce – than others.

span.label: selection - ontogenetic: consequences shaping behaviour within one animal's lifetime
span.quote: These examples are instances of ontogenetic selection, that is guidance by consequences during the life of the individual.

span.label: selection - phylogenetic: consequences shaping a species over evolutionary time
span.quote: There is also phylogenetic selection – selection during the evolution of the species.

span.label: conditioning - operant: the animal has control, and outcomes are contingent on its behaviour
span.quote: The distinction between Pavlovian and operant conditioning therefore rests on whether the animal only observes the relationships between events in the world (in Pavlovian conditioning), or whether it also has some control over their occurrence (in operant conditioning).

span.label: conditioning - Pavlovian: the animal only observes, and no response is required for the outcome
span.quote: Unlike operant conditioning, in classical conditioning no response is required to get the food.

span.label: contradicts → Herrnstein's matching law (Richard Herrnstein, 1961), as a general law relating response rate to reinforcement rate
span.quote: Although postulated as a general law relating response rate and reinforcement rate, it turned out that the matching relationship is actually far from being universally true.

span.label: builds-on → Thorndike's Law of Effect
span.quote: The scientific study of operant conditioning dates from the beginning of the twentieth century with the work of Edward L. Thorndike in the U.S. and C. Lloyd Morgan in the U.K.

span.label: contradicts → Skinner's framework as a theory in the ordinary sense

span.label: instrumental conditioning —same-as→ operant conditioning
span.quote: Operant conditioning (also known as instrumental conditioning ) is a process by which humans and animals learn to behave in such a way as to obtain rewards and avoid punishments.

span.label: ontogenetic selection —same-as→ operant conditioning
span.quote: Other names for ontogenetic selection are instrumental or operant (B. F. Skinner’s term) conditioning.

span.label: operant conditioning —distinct-from→ Pavlovian conditioning
span.quote: Unlike operant conditioning, in classical conditioning no response is required to get the food.

span.label: ontogenetic selection —contrasted-with→ phylogenetic selection
span.quote: There is also phylogenetic selection – selection during the evolution of the species.

span.label: reinforcer —contrasted-with→ punisher
span.quote: In general, a consequence is called a reinforcer if it strengthens the behavior that led to it, and it is a punisher if it weakens that behavior.

span.label: reinforcer —part-of→ contingency
span.quote: Reinforcement is the selective agent, acting via temporal contiguity (the sooner the reinforcer follows the response, the greater its effect), frequency (the more often these pairings occur the better) and contingency (how well does the target response predict the reinforcer).

span.label: Adding free food that arrives independently of the rat's lever pressing makes the rat press less, not more, because the response no longer predicts food as well.
span.quote: Suppose we now give additional food pellets on a random basis, independent of the animal’s lever pressing. Will he press more, or less? The answer is less.

span.label: Matching is not a general law of behaviour but a by-product of the negative feedback built into concurrent variable-interval schedules, so observing matching identifies no particular learning process.
span.quote: In fact, the matching relationship can be seen as a result of the negative-feedback properties of the choice situation (concurrent variable-interval schedule) in which it is measured.

span.label: Matching depends on the animal's switching history: pigeons trained on each option separately and only then given the choice abandon matching and respond exclusively to the richer schedule.
span.quote: If pigeons are first trained to each choice separately then allowed to choose, they do not match, they pick the richer schedule exclusively.

span.label: Reversibility of steady-state performance is misleading — an animal returned to a schedule performs the same way but is not in the same state, as extinction and transfer tests between groups reveal.
span.quote: Finally, the fact that steady-state behavior is often reversible does not mean that the animal’s state is equally reversible.

span.label: The field concentrated almost entirely on how reinforcement strengthens behaviour and neglected where the reinforced behaviour comes from in the first place — the problem of behavioural variation.
span.quote: almost all operant-conditioning research has been focused on the strengthening effect of reinforcement and almost none on the question of origins, where the behavior comes from in the first place

span.label: Both stimulus-response and action-outcome control structures have been demonstrated to exist, which is exactly the basis for splitting operant behaviour into habitual and goal-directed classes.
span.quote: Research in the last two decades has convincingly shown that both types of control structures exist.

span.label: Autoshaping shows behaviour can be generated before any operant reinforcement: a pigeon comes to peck a key that merely predicts food, and keeps pecking it even when pecking cancels the food.
span.quote: Eventually, the pigeon is likely to peck the key even if a contingency is set up such that key-pecking causes the removal of the food.

span.label: Dopamine is identified as the neural carrier of a reward prediction error delivered to basal ganglia targets, linking reinforcement-learning models to brain data.
span.quote: much evidence suggests that the neuromodulator dopamine provides basal ganglia target structures with a reward prediction error that can influence learning and action selection

span.label: Because operant behaviour appears even in bacteria and possibly protists, the essentials of operant conditioning cannot require any particular neural machinery.
span.quote: certainly a simple kind of operant behavior, if not discrimination learning, occurs even in bacteria. Thus, the essentials of operant conditioning need not depend on specific neural structures.

span.label: Behaviour guided by consequences is universal across animals, from protists to humans.
span.quote: The behavior of all animals, from protists to humans, is guided by its consequences.

span.label: Adding reward that is NOT contingent on the response reduces responding - the animal tracks predictiveness, not frequency of pairing.
span.quote: Lever pressing is less predictive of food than it was before, because food sometimes occurs at other times.

span.label: The field's own gap, stated plainly: research has studied how responses are strengthened and almost never where they come from.
